title: American Black Duck
summary: Black ducks connect Long Island marshes with Shinnecock waterfowl knowledge and the art of decoy carving.
content:
Between marsh, water, and sky

The American black duck (Anas rubripes) is a native waterbird of Long Island. Wertheim National Wildlife Refuge describes black ducks gathering on open water, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service identifies coastal salt marshes as important habitat. These ducks swim and fly between feeding and resting places.[1][2]

Shinnecock knowledge of waterfowl

The Shinnecock Elders’ resource catalogue lists black ducks among local waterfowl. Its broader waterfowl account describes decoys made from reeds and later carving in wood, naming Charles Sumner Bunn and Lyle G. Smith as Shinnecock carvers.[3]

Recognizing the maker

Charles Sumner Bunn’s work connects bird observation with skilled carving. Shelburne Museum’s exhibition In Plain Sight: Rediscovering Charles Sumner Bunn’s Decoys examines the attribution of decoys to this Shinnecock maker. Recognizing an artist’s name restores a human history to objects that may once have been discussed mainly as collectibles.[4]

Continue with Charles Sumner Bunn’s biography to explore his life and connections.

Look at shape and movement

Watch how a duck holds its head, floats, and lifts into flight. Which details would a carver need to notice? The map’s flying silhouette offers a starting point; the wetlands and the art each tell more of the story.

The moving animal is an illustration of habitat and movement, not a live sighting or a route to wildlife.

why_this_matters: Wetlands sustain birds and the cultural knowledge connected with them. Shinnecock decoy carving shows how close observation can become art, livelihood, and a legacy whose makers deserve recognition.
